meta.title: Icelandic A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Icelandic → English (see the Icelandic, recall the meaning) and English → Icelandic (see an English meaning, recall the Icelandic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words of Icelandic for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters, and to describe in simple terms aspects of their background, immediate environment and matters in areas of immediate need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded word list for Icelandic as a foreign language was found published, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 271 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the seasons and dates, more numbers, the land and nature, the weather, animals, clothes, the home and the kitchen, food and cooking, work and jobs, school, travel and transport, the town, health, feelings, free time, the everyday verbs of these, describing things and people, time words, and the words that join one clause to the next — and the other 479 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Icelandic, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Icelandic has no word for 'a', so the 362 nouns carry their gender beside their meaning — masculine, feminine or neuter, which decides every ending the noun and its adjective take — and show the forms a dictionary gives a noun by: the definite (the article is an ending: hesturinn, 'the horse'), the genitive singular and the plural (hests, hestar); behind the All forms fold are its four cases, nominative, accusative, dative and genitive, in both numbers. The 193 verbs show their present 'he' form, past and supine (fer, fór, farið — the forms an Icelandic verb is learnt by), and behind the fold the present in all six persons, the past plural, the past participle and the imperative. Adjectives show their three genders and their comparison. Real example sentences come with 676 of the 750 words, three apiece for 561 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and the forms of nouns, adjectives and pronouns, and the past and supine of verbs: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). The present tense and imperative of verbs: The Database of Icelandic Morphology (Beygingarlýsing íslensks nútímamáls). The Árni Magnússon Institute for Icelandic Studies. Author and editor Kristín Bjarnadóttir. https://bin.arnastofnun.is (CC BY-SA 4.0) — six present forms and the imperative are taken for each verb, unchanged; nothing else is used. Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0), whose mis-encoded letters (đ for ð, ū for þ) were mapped back before counting. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
